svg.title: DevOps Principles
svg.desc: A3 landscape reference poster: the three ways of DevOps (flow, feedback, continual learning) with a question, practices and toolkit tools for each, a CALMS health check, the four key delivery metrics, and four DevOps habits.
svg.text: Build, release and run software as one team: fast flow to customers, fast feedback from them, and a habit of learning.
Engineering Practices · Inspired by The DevOps Handbook (Kim, Humble, Debois, Willis) and Accelerate (Forsgren, Humble, Kim)
Speed up the whole path from idea to customer: small batches, visible work, fewer
hand-offs, and never passing a known problem downstream.
“How long does a small change take to reach a customer?”
Make the work visible, end to end
Find problems fast and close to where they start: automated tests, monitoring, and
teams who see how their work behaves in production.
“How soon would we know if a release hurt customers?”
Fix the cause, then add a check
Treat failures as information, run small experiments, and set time aside to improve
daily work and share what you learn.
“What did our last incident teach us, and what changed?”
FIVE PARTS OF DEVOPS · WHICH IS WEAKEST HERE?
Shared ownership of building and running the work, with trust and no
Developers and operations solve incidents together.
Automate the repetitive and risky steps: build, test, deploy and
Any change can reach production through one pipeline.
Small batches, limited work in progress, and less waste on the way to
Changes are small, and merged at least daily.
Measure flow, quality and outcomes, and use them to learn, not to
The team knows how long changes take and how often they fail.
Share tools, knowledge and lessons across teams and roles.
Incident reviews and runbooks are open to everyone.
CALMS was set out by Jez Humble, building on CAMS from John Willis and Damon Edwards. Score each part 1–5 as a team, then improve the lowest.

How fast service recovers after a failure

svg.text: Speed and stability go together. Track them on Delivery Metrics.
You build it, you run it
The team that builds a service helps support it.
Smaller releases are easier to test and undo.
Turn a repeated manual step into a script.
Ask what made the mistake easy, not who made it.
“Where does a change wait longest on its way to customers?”
